text: Doomformer compiles integer neural networks into ZDoom maps and runs them in ViZDoom. Voodoo dolls (the copies of the player that DOOM spawns for extra player-1 starts) do the arithmetic, and sector light levels and plane heights hold the sums. Python reads every exposed value back from the running game and compares it with a NumPy integer reference, tolerance 0. One value off by one and the run fails. It is slow: about 23,000 times slower than NumPy on a small MLP (engine time; 65,000 times with a timer around the whole call), and a handwritten digit takes 163 seconds of real-time DOOM in one map at the default schedule and 8 seconds at --opt 3 . Install · Proof · How it works · Films · Docs pip install git+https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer # Python 3.11+, Linux or macOS doomformer hello # 2 s: a small MLP, every value checked doomformer draw --digit 7 # 15 s: the marine walks a 7 and the level reads it doomformer doctor checks ViZDoom, Freedoom and the display, builds ACC if it is absent, and compiles an ACS probe before reporting success. The first build needs git , cmake , a C compiler and network access to github.com. Linux uses dynamic runtimes: glibc-static is not required. On Fedora: sudo dnf install git cmake gcc gcc-c++ make . The Colab notebook needs no setup, but you draw on a browser canvas and doomformer mnist --image feeds it to DOOM, with no marine. Holding FIRE, the marine inks a 3×3 brush of floor cells under him. READ makes the level write the 784 pixels into the network, and 1,355 voodoo dolls in the same map compute it. With --digit , Python stands in for you: it presses the marine's keys and USE once, then only advances the clock and reads. ▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄ ▄████████████████ ████▀▀ ▀████▀ ▀▀▀ ▄███▀ ████ ███ ███ ███ ████ ███▀ ████ ▀███ DOOM reads: 7 (right) -- the winner's doll lit it on the 7-segment display EXACT: all 248 values DOOM computed [...] equal the NumPy integer reference (tolerance 0) READ pass: 273 game tics = 8 s of real-time DOOM at 35 tics/s, 3 s wall [...] Abridged at [...] ; docs/commands.md has the whole output. draw builds its map with --opt 3 , so a READ takes 273 game tics; at --opt 0 , the original schedule, it takes 5,705 (163 s of real-time DOOM). Without --digit the command opens a window and you walk and draw yourself; DOOM then runs in real time. The dolls compute 784 pixels → 64 hidden units → 45 pairwise score comparisons → 10 win counts. Only the digit that wins all nine of its comparisons gets a doll through, and the line that doll crosses starts the level script that lights the digit on the display. Python reads back the 784 pixels, the hidden layer, every comparison and the answer and checks all 248 values (119 values, each read with its negated twin, plus 10 outputs). EXACT means DOOM equals the integer network. It says nothing about whether the digit is right. On the first 100 MNIST test digits DOOM reads 99 correctly, and 966 of 1,000 sampled from all 10,000; every result is exact. The integer network scores 97.16 % on all 10,000 (the float model scores 97.58 %). The 30 walked digits (0 to 9, three scripted stroke variants each) all read correctly and exact at --opt 3 , and the network is also trained on that stroke distribution: the first version of this demo, a 784-32-10 network trained on MNIST alone, reads only 41.08 % of such strokes. Through real X key events a drawn 7 read exact at the default --opt 3 ; a 7 and a 1 were tried at --opt 0 with an earlier network. Details · film doomformer museum build writes museum.wad , a map you can play without Python. You step on seven floor pads to light a digit and press READ. 136 voodoo dolls compute a small hand-written network: each digit's score counts the segments that agree with it, and the winner's doll lights the display. MUTATE rewires one connection of that network inside the running level: segment a to digit 7 goes from +1 to -1, by changing the specials of its two weight lines. The same 7 then reads as 1, and RESTORE puts it back. The HUD and a scoreboard show the ten scores after each READ, and a camera station shows digit 7's sixth score doll: it passes its gate before MUTATE and stops in front of it after. $ doomformer museum verify 7 pads abc w_7a +1 DOOM reads 7 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) 7 after MUTATE pads abc w_7a -1 DOOM reads 1 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) 7 after RESTORE pads abc w_7a +1 DOOM reads 7 scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4] EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...]) Here Python plays: it presses the marine's keys and USE, and during each READ it only reads, with guarded readouts. It compares all 148 values with the NumPy reference of the network as it is wired at that moment. Without running DOOM, the static extractor also shows that the rewired map's netlist is the network with exactly that one weight changed. I have run the whole map only in ViZDoom. Its self-test map reads the digits 0 to 9, then the 7 after MUTATE and after RESTORE, without a player. On a GitHub runner it logs the exact values in GZDoom 4.14.2, LZDoom 3.88b, UZDoom 5.0.3 and ZDoom 2.8.1, and in Zandronum 3.2.1 only when every sector tag is below 32,768. Details Python reads sector light levels and floor and ceiling heights from the running game and compares each with an independent NumPy integer implementation of the same network. The check is integer equality over the runs that were made, and says nothing about inputs that were not run. The tests attack it: raising one weight line in a small compiled map from 5 to 6 must fail by exactly +1 on exactly the inputs whose dolls cross that line, and a readout that echoes a value Python wrote must fail ( pytest tests/test_tamper.py , three tests, about 15 s). Readback is guarded by default: before each page, Python poisons and checks its USER slots, then requires the page to replace them. Dropping a page cannot silently reuse a repeated input's answer or the previous page's values. guard=False is an explicit one-map historical opt-out. Guarded builds have new hashes (ACS and metadata, not geometry or arithmetic); the hash record explains the change. doomformer fuzz --nets 40 compares every value of 40 random nets run in DOOM (306 passes, 0 mismatches, about 10 s with --workers 2 ; a planted compiler bug is found). fuzz --edge puts weights, biases and inputs at the range limits: 15,000 nets over ten fresh seeds, at --opt 0 , at --opt 3 and as tile maps, made 113,605 passes and compared 1,987,632 values with no mismatch (the range check refused 47,686 of the inputs it drew, about 30 %), 3,000 more with the generator widened to plane starts near the bounds below (22,682 passes) and 2,000 more that also draw starts from 15,000 to 16,000 (14,782 passes), all with no mismatch. Earlier campaigns ran 2,000 random MLPs (15,374 passes, 276,594 values), 300 spiking nets and 100 random transformers over all 8 attention, norm and MLP variants (99 ran; one all-zero matrix is unsupported), after the scheduling fixes; 200 spiking --edge nets made 12,794 passes with no mismatch. fuzz --edge does not draw transformers. CI fuzzes 60 nets with a fresh, printed seed on every push and a longer campaign every Monday. The fuzzer and independent runs found four faults in this repo's own maps: two scheduling bugs and two plane limits. A plane move that starts more than 14,018 units from zero keeps its mover busy for three tics and drops the next request on that plane, and a plane that starts above 16,000 is exact on the first pass and wrong on later ones, so DOOM disagreed with the reference on nets that net.check had accepted. check and compile now refuse them: planes start inside [-15,000, 16,000] and move within ±14,018 ( doomformer verify --plane-sweep , docs/verification.md ). doomformer verify runs every input class of a small MLP (the classes agree with every input on 20 of 20 nets, under an assumption stated in the same page). df.coverage counts what is compared: on MNIST all 248 exposed values, which are 129 values the reference defines and 119 twins, and the count falls when a readout name is dropped. The map does not expose the 903 staircase counts and 1,351 gate comparisons of the same net; they are checked through the sums they feed. doomformer verify --extract net.wad --net net.npz reads the net back out of a compiled map without starting DOOM and compares every weight, bias and threshold with the source net: the shipped MNIST net (784-64-45-10-10) comes back equal from its map alone at --opt 0 to 3, and so do 484 of 490 random nets at --opt 0 (the other 6 are equal but break the plane contract) and 199 of 199 at each of --opt 1 to 3. EQUAL covers the arithmetic netlist, the plane contract, the trigger and repeat flags, the mover speeds, the reset script and the readout pages; timing and geometry are printed as NOT CHECKED. A changed weight line shows as exactly that weight. Of 23,622 single edits to a small map at --opt 0 the extractor detects 17,906, and the 98 undetected edits that were run in DOOM on 12 inputs were all exact. It shows what the map says; that DOOM runs the map as read is what the exactness checks test. A mutation harness changes one line of a compiled map: of the 1,004 sites run (of 5,578) 297 are killed, all weight, sign and target classes among them. Of the 707 survivors 590 match a rule (a redundant scroller, a freeze line a forward pass never needs) that aggregate controls support, and 117 are input gaps (walking floors that only some inputs expose); none is proven equivalent. doomformer lint --fuzz compared the static schedule checker with DOOM on 5,397 maps: 0 false negatives. The method is translation validation (Pnueli, Siegel and Singerman, 1998): a test of each compile, not a proof that the compiler is right. Who does what: In the draw , his brain, loop, fly and machine runs a wrapper ( ReadoutOnly ) makes any other call raise, and the commands are counted: 58 in a headless draw pass, 710 in the film run of his brain, 154 in the lesion run, 0 others. The maps use ZDoom's UDMF format and ACS, so they need ZDoom (here ViZDoom 1.3.2 with Freedoom assets), not the 1993 executable. net.quantization_report(x) measures how far an integer model is from the float model it came from. EXACT does not. docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md maps each part of a network to a part of the map: a value to a group of dolls, a weight to a line, an activation to a staircase, attention to a corridor of ceiling gates, ablation to a door. The engine has sharp edges and the compiler works around them. A plane mover refuses a second request on the same plane for as long as the first is still moving, and the later one is lost. A teleport line cancels the lines a doll crossed earlier in that tic. A thing more than 32,767 units from a BSP node can be filed under the wrong sector, so every map fits 32,000 units. These are ZDoom 2.8.1 behaviours measured in ViZDoom 1.3.2. The 32,000-unit rule is needed on Linux; on macOS arm64 the wrap did not occur in the probe maps (cause not investigated), and the rule is kept everywhere. The exported probe maps and the hello brain also ran in stock ZDoom 2.8.1 (53 of 53 rows match), Zandronum 3.2.1 (50 of 53: it cannot find sector tags above 32,767) and GZDoom 4.14.2, LZDoom and UZDoom (44 of 53: planes are doubles there and the UDMF parser refuses coordinates beyond ±32,768; the coordinate wrap stays). The hello brain's logged values equal the NumPy reference in ZDoom, GZDoom, LZDoom and UZDoom, and in Zandronum once its tags are moved below 32,768. The doll-clock counter machine ( multiply 7 9 , 464 steps, 235,567 tics) and a SUBLEQ add also ran in GZDoom, LZDoom and UZDoom with every step's pc and registers equal to the interpreter's log; ZDoom 2.8.1 and Zandronum (tags below 32,768) ran a 50-step multiply and the SUBLEQ add exactly, and stalled Zandronum with default tags at step 1 ( Other ports ). doomformer facts re-runs 28 probes (55 cases) with PASS or FAIL per row (about 10 s), and Engine facts lists each finding with the probe or test behind it. Computers inside DOOM maps exist already. counter.wad (2006) is a 4-bit counter built from voodoo dolls and conveyor belts, conway.wad runs Game of Life in a Boom map, and Danny Spencer's DOOM calculator is an adding machine. Doomformer adds a compiler from integer networks to ZDoom maps, a measured list of engine behaviours that break exactness, and a tolerance-0 check against a NumPy reference. docs/related_work.md lists what was opened and what each entry shares and does not. hello runs a 4-6-5-3 integer MLP, demo is a 1-layer transformer trained on 136 official level names cut into 38 tile maps, --nightmare is the 2-layer model (56,390 dolls), and ask is a 2-layer transformer trained on 189 DOOM facts. docs/commands.md has every command and variant with sample output: mnist --image and --tiles , demo --softmax , --model doomnames_modern , --one-map , --loop , --opt , fuzz , verify , lint , tune , facts , machine , learn . Times are from an idle 16-core arm64 Linux machine running up to 8 games at once; hello and draw use one game. With 2 games, demo took about 1 minute and demo --softmax about 3.5 minutes on a busy machine, and ask took 20 minutes on 3 games. His brain is the level. A level script senses the nearest demon, 1,345 voodoo dolls of the marine run his policy transformer and pick the action, and the level turns him and pulls the trigger. Python advances the clock and reads. 50 of 50 decisions exact (seed 4). A decision takes 4,338 game tics (124 s of real-time DOOM); with --opt 3 the same 50 decisions pick the same 50 actions, all exact, in 774 tics (22 s) each. In that run his dolls turn for 21 decisions while the first demon is far away, first choose FIRE at decision 22, and choose it five times in all; five demons die. The policy imitates a scripted aimbot that sees exact demon positions. The demons are frozen while he thinks, and with them awake ( --live , below) he is dead after 5.5 s with 0 kills, which the arena nearly forces; the film time-lapses the thinking. Film · code Run the experiments from a clone ( pip install -e . , then python -m demos.<name> ). demos/README.md lists each command, its time and what it prints: The showreel covers all of them. docs/DEMOS.md has the numbers, the scope of each check and the list of picked seeds, and docs/FLY.md covers the fly. Compile a network into a map and let its outputs open doors, flash lights or shove the marine. This runs as pasted: import numpy as np import doomformer as df # 2 inputs -> [a AND b, a OR b] -> 2 outputs, all integers net = df . MLP ( weights = [ np . array ([[ 1 , 1 ], [ 1 , 1 ]]), np . array ([[ 1 , 0 ], [ 0 , 1 ]])], biases = [ np . array ([ - 1 , 0 ]), np . array ([ 0 , 0 ])], thresholds = [ np . array ([ 1 ]), np . array ([ 1 ])], signed_input = False , ) with df . compile ( net ) as brain : for x in ([ 0 , 0 ], [ 1 , 0 ], [ 1 , 1 ]): # computed by voodoo dolls; raises df.MismatchError on any difference from net.reference print ( x , "->" , brain ( np . array ( x )). tolist ()) brain . record ([ np . array ([ 0 , 1 ]), np . array ([ 1 , 1 ])], "dolls.gif" ) # film the dolls doing it df.MLP.from_torch quantises a PyTorch model ( example 02 ), and the world and actions hooks put rooms in the map and attach doors, lights and thrusts to the outputs ( example 03 ). The same API takes spiking networks, transformers, Conv1d and Conv2d, and learners that update their weights inside the map; mode="tiles" spreads a model over a pool of games ( doomformer plan tells you which case you have). The guide is docs/BUILD_YOUR_OWN.md , and there are twelve one-file examples . Built something odd? Show and tell . One map is one game, and one game uses one core. df.run_many gives each input to the next idle game, checks every pass and returns the outputs in order, on your machine or on a Ray cluster you start. Nothing is hosted. 1,000 MNIST test digits in 14 games on one 16-core machine took 2 hours: 966 read correctly, all 1,000 exact, 5,696,000 game tics or 45 hours of real-time DOOM ( models/mnist/doom_1000.json ). Tiles are the multi-map design: four tile maps, one per layer, in resident games, with Python copying the layer values from one game to the next. doomformer mnist --tiles --all --workers 6 read all 10,000 test digits in 1,390 s: 10,000 of 10,000 exact (248 values each), 9,716 right (97.16 %), DOOM's one-hot equal to NumPy's on every digit ( models/mnist/doom_tiles_10000.json ). A digit takes 216 game tics and 0.83 s there against 5,696 tics and about 104 s in one map. doomformer plan predicts seconds (rms error 13 % for one map and 22 % for tiles on 11 held-out K3 and K8 nets; on nets of other K the measured seconds were 0 to 40 % above the prediction, and 21 % above for MNIST at --opt 0 ), prints game tics with an error band (276 ± 7.2 % for MNIST at --opt 3 , 272 measured) and recommends one. doomformer bench tiles reads MNIST at 81 digits per minute with 1 worker and 880 with 16 (steady state; 79 and 552 with game start), every pass exact, at 0.72 s of engine CPU per digit with 1 worker and 0.92 s with 16 (100 shipped digits, twice; 16 cores). doomformer mnist --tiles --all --workers 6 # all 10,000 digits as tile maps, about 23 min pip install " doomformer[ray] " ray start --head # other machines: ray start --address=HEAD:6379 doomformer mnist --all --ray --record mnist.json # all 10,000 digits, one map each, on a cluster Budget one core and about 1.3 GB of RAM per game (measured peak 1.24 GB). docs/scaling.md has the measurements.
